summary: This draft standard revises and extends the vendor information fields of BOOTP, the protocol a diskless machine uses to learn its network settings at startup. It adds new tags, such as for a domain name, and builds on the earlier work in RFC 1048. It was replaced by RFC 1497 and RFC 1533.

eli5.summary: When a computer wakes up knowing nothing, it asks the network for its settings. This paper lists extra labelled facts the answer can include, like the name of its neighborhood.

questions: what does bootp vendor info field contain
subtitle: Extensible configuration parameters for diskless computers at boot time.

tldr.problem: Diskless machines need to obtain not just an IP address but also gateway addresses, server addresses, and other network configuration when they boot.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 1395 extends BOOTP's vendor information field with a set of tagged, length-encoded fields that can carry subnet masks, gateway addresses, domain names, server addresses, and other configuration parameters.
tldr.outcome: BOOTP servers can now supply a full set of network configuration in a single reply, eliminating the need for multiple protocol exchanges. It was later superseded by RFC 1497 and RFC 1533.

today: RFC 1497 and RFC 1533 superseded this RFC with more complete vendor information specifications. This RFC is no longer the current standard for BOOTP vendor extensions.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 1395 defines vendor-specific information extensions for the Bootstrap Protocol (BOOTP). It builds on earlier work in RFC 1048 and extends BOOTP with additional configuration parameters that diskless machines need at boot time.

As networks grew and workstations proliferated, the administrative burden of configuring each host individually became impractical. The problem was especially acute for diskless machines that had no local storage to hold configuration information. BOOTP provided a solution for assigning IP addresses, but networks needed a way to distribute additional parameters such as gateway addresses, server locations, and domain names from a centralized point.
sections.eli5: BOOTP lets computers ask the network for their settings. This document adds extra labels so the answer can include more information, like which servers to use.

sections.title: BOOTP Overview
sections.content:
BOOTP (Bootstrap Protocol) is a UDP/IP-based protocol that allows a booting host to configure itself dynamically without user intervention. It provides a means to assign a host its IP address, a boot file location and server address, and optionally the address of an Internet gateway. This allows centralized management of network addresses and boot images for potentially hundreds of hosts.

Rather than maintaining unique configuration files for each host, administrators can categorize hosts into classes and maintain configuration information for each class. This dramatically reduces the complexity of network administration at scale.
sections.eli5: A booting computer sends one message asking the network for its settings. A BOOTP server replies with the computer's IP address and other information it needs to get started.

sections.title: Vendor Information Format
sections.content:
BOOTP packets contain a 64-octet vendor information field, initially unspecified. RFC 1395 defines how to use this field with a generalized format that works across different machine types and operating systems.

The vendor information begins with a four-octet magic cookie with the value 99.130.83.99 (hexadecimal 63.82.53.63) in network byte order. This magic cookie identifies that the following data uses the tagged format defined in this RFC. Individual fields are length-tagged, allowing clients to skip fields they do not understand. All multi-byte quantities use network byte order.

Fields fall into two categories: fixed-length fields with no data (pad and end markers) and variable-length fields containing data. Each field consists of a tag octet, a length octet (for variable fields), and the data.
sections.eli5: The vendor information is a labeled list, like a shipping label with fields for address, phone, special instructions. Each label has a tag number, a length, and the information. Unknown labels can be skipped safely.

sections.title: Configuration Parameters
sections.content:
RFC 1395 defines 18 information tags (0-17), with reserved tags 128-254 for site-specific extensions. Key parameters include:

  • Subnet Mask (tag 1): The net and local subnet mask.
  • Gateway Addresses (tag 3): IP addresses of gateways for this subnet.
  • Domain Name Servers (tag 6): IP addresses of DNS servers for domain name resolution.
  • Hostname (tag 12): The name of the client.
  • Domain Name (tag 15): The client's domain for DNS resolution.
  • Root Path (tag 17): A pathname to mount as the root disk for diskless systems.
  • Time Servers, Log Servers, and LPR Servers: Various service addresses for network resources.

Additional parameters like time offset, boot file size, swap server address, and others are available. Administrators must be careful not to exceed the 64-byte length restriction by including only essential information.
sections.eli5: The tags are like labeled boxes: one box holds the gateway address, another holds the domain name, another holds the list of nameservers. The booting computer opens only the boxes it needs.

sections.title: Extensions and Site-Specific Use
sections.content:
The RFC includes a process for registering additional generic data fields through IANA. Implementation-specific use of undefined generic types (those in the range 18-127) may conflict with other implementations and requires registration with IANA to avoid collision.

Reserved tags 128-254 are designated for site-specific information interpreted on an implementation-specific basis. This allows organizations to add custom configuration parameters without conflicting with standardized tags.
sections.eli5: If you want to add a new type of information, you can register it with IANA to get an official tag number. If you just want to use something locally, you can pick a number above 127.

items.label: Subnet Mask
items.desc: The subnet mask for IP subnetting.

items.label: Gateway Addresses
items.desc: IP addresses of routers for this subnet.

items.label: Root Path
items.desc: Pathname to mount as root disk.
